alignment.note: The Greek opens with the connective Καὶ and the Vulgate with Et; the Peshitta omits the initial conjunction, preferring to begin the clause asyndetically with the verb ܐܡܪ, a common Syriac narrative pattern.

Greek uses the historic present λέγει ('says') while the Vulgate ait and the Peshitta perfect ܐܡܪ ('said') render it as a past; both versions normalise the Markan vivid present into a simple narrative past tense.

The emphatic Greek subject pronoun αὐτὸς ('he himself') is left untranslated in both the Peshitta and the Vulgate, which let the verbal inflection carry the subject; the Peshitta instead supplies the explicit name ܝܫܘܥ.
αὐτοῖς / ܠܗܘܢ / illis (the dative/preposition-marked indirect object 'to them'); the Vulgate adds the colon as discourse punctuation.
The Peshitta makes the subject explicit by inserting the proper name ܝܫܘܥ ('Jesus'), a frequent Syriac clarifying expansion where the Greek relies only on the pronoun αὐτὸς.
οὐδέποτε / ܠܐ ܡܡܬܘܡ / Numquam ('never'); Syriac expresses the single Greek adverb with the negative particle ܠܐ plus ܡܡܬܘܡ.

Greek ἐποίησεν and Peshitta ܥܒܕ are indicative aorist/perfect ('did'), whereas the Vulgate fecerit is subjunctive, reflecting Latin's preference for the subjunctive in indirect questions introduced by quid.

Greek and Latin use a noun-plus-verb periphrasis (χρείαν ἔσχεν / necessitatem habuit, 'had need'); the Peshitta condenses this into the single verb ܐܣܬܢܩ ('he was in need'), an Ethpaal denominative idiom.
καί / et (the coordinating conjunction 'and'); the Peshitta prefixes this conjunction proclitically as the waw of ܘܟܦܢ rather than as a separate token.
ἐπείνασεν / ܘܟܦܢ / esuriit ('and he hungered'); the Syriac waw of conjunction is fused to the verb.

Greek uses an articular prepositional phrase (οἱ μετ᾽ αὐτοῦ, 'those with him') and the Vulgate a relative clause with explicit verb (qui cum eo erant); the Peshitta compresses the whole phrase into the prefixed relative-plus-preposition form ܘܕܥܡܗ ('and those who were with him'), semantically equivalent but markedly more economical.
The Vulgate closes with an explicit question mark, matching the Greek interrogative αὐτοῦ;; the Peshitta carries no terminal punctuation token in this edition.
